questions.question: 1. Which of the following is an advantage of using a hash table for storing key-value pairs?

answers.a: It always keeps the keys sorted.
answers.b: It can provide average-case constant-time lookup.
answers.c: It requires every key to have the same value.
answers.d: It eliminates the possibility of collisions.

explanations.a: Incorrect. A standard hash table does not maintain its keys in sorted order.
explanations.b: Correct. With a suitable hash function and a controlled load factor, lookup in a hash table is typically O(1) on average.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A hash table is designed to associate potentially different keys with their corresponding values.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Different keys can produce the same hash-table index, so collisions are possible.

questions.question: 2. What happens when two different keys are mapped to the same index by a hash function?

answers.a: The hash table is automatically sorted.
answers.b: The second key is always discarded.
answers.c: A collision occurs and a collision-resolution method is required.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Mapping two keys to the same index does not cause the hash table to become sorted.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A collision does not necessarily mean that the second key must be discarded; collision-resolution techniques can be used.
explanations.c: Correct. When two different keys map to the same table index, a collision occurs and the hash table must resolve it using a suitable technique.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A collision is a normal possibility in hashing and does not by itself make the hash function invalid.

questions.question: 3. What is the expected average-case time complexity of searching for a key in a well-designed hash table?

explanations.a: Correct. Under a good hash function and a suitable load factor, a hash-table search takes O(1) time on average.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Logarithmic search is characteristic of structures such as balanced search trees rather than the expected average case of a well-designed hash table.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A linear search may occur in an unfavorable hash-table situation, but it is not the expected average-case complexity.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Quadratic time is not the expected average-case complexity of hash-table search.

questions.question: 4. In which of the following applications can hash tables be used?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Hash tables are commonly used for associative arrays, so selecting only this option does not account for the other valid applications.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Hash tables can implement symbol tables, but this is not the only valid application listed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Hash tables are useful for dictionaries and key-value mappings, but other listed applications are also valid.
explanations.d: Correct. Hash tables are widely used to implement associative arrays, symbol tables, dictionaries, and other key-value mappings.

questions.question: 5. Consider a hash table containing $n$ elements. If all keys happen to be mapped to the same index and collisions are handled using separate chaining, what can be the worst-case time complexity of searching for a key?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A chain containing all $n$ elements does not provide logarithmic search time.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Constant-time search is the expected goal under good distribution, but it is not guaranteed when all keys collide.
explanations.c: Correct. If all $n$ keys are placed in one chain, searching that chain can require examining O(n) elements.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Searching a single chain containing $n$ elements does not require a quadratic number of comparisons.

questions.question: 6. What is the load factor of a hash table with $n$ stored elements and table size $m$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Reversing the number of stored elements and table size gives the reciprocal of the usual load-factor definition.
explanations.b: Correct. The load factor is defined as $\alpha = n/m$, where $n$ is the number of stored elements and $m$ is the table size.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Load factor is a ratio, not the sum of the number of elements and table size.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Subtracting the table size from the number of elements does not define the load factor.

questions.question: 7. Which property is most desirable for a hash function used in a hash table?

answers.a: It should map every key to index 0.
answers.b: It should preserve the alphabetical order of keys.
answers.c: It should distribute keys uniformly across the table.
answers.d: It should always produce a unique index for every possible key.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Mapping every key to the same index would create excessive collisions.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Preserving key order is not the primary purpose of a hash function.
explanations.c: Correct. A good hash function distributes keys as uniformly as possible to reduce collisions and improve performance.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A hash table usually has fewer indices than the number of possible keys, so collisions cannot always be avoided.

questions.question: 8. Suppose the hash function is $h(k) = k \bmod 10$. What index is produced for the key $37$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The remainder after dividing 37 by 10 is not 3.
explanations.b: Correct. Since $37 \bmod 10 = 7$, the key is mapped to index 7.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The modulo operation produces a remainder from 0 through 9 for a divisor of 10.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The hash function transforms the key using the modulo operation rather than returning the original key.

questions.question: 9. Why can a hash table have $O(n)$ worst-case search time even though its expected search time is often $O(1)$?

answers.a: Because a poor distribution of keys can cause many collisions.
answers.b: Because hash-table indices are always searched in sorted order.
answers.c: Because every hash-table operation must inspect all table positions.
answers.d: Because the table size is always equal to one.

explanations.a: Correct. If many keys collide at the same location, a search may need to examine many entries, producing O(n) worst-case time.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Hash tables do not require their indices or keys to be searched in sorted order.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A well-designed hash table does not normally inspect every table position for each operation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A table can have many positions; the worst case is related to collisions rather than a table size of one.
